messages.author: a8b6459b77c849fe
messages.subject: Parallelizing individual chains
parts:
What do you all see as the issues involved in attempting to parallelize individual chains in Stan?

I understand that the MCMC iterations are inherently sequential, as are the simulation steps within an iteration, so I'm looking at speeding up the gradient computations. Even, say, a 2X speedup using 3 cores would be of great interest to me.

I'm assuming that users would have to indicate where parallelism is to be used in writing the model -- perhaps something like a parallel for loop.

I've written custom MCMC code using multiple cores before, focusing on speeding up the individual iterations. If it can be done in a reasonable amount of time (say, two weeks of focused effort, not months), there's a good chance my employer will okay me taking the time to work on adding to Stan the capability to make use of multiple cores.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Parallelizing individual chains
parts:
The issue that makes it hard is that autodiff is inherently
sequential as currently written. But given that autodiff,
like the density functions themselves, will be a big sparse
sum, there’s certainly hope.

Kevin — I’ll send you a draft of the autodiff paper off list
(the source is on a branch in stan-dev/stan), which
provides an overview of how it currently works. I have put
zero thought into parallelizing it, though it would be a big
deal if someone could figure it out.

There are ways to factor a directed graphical model, but
I think you’re right that for Stan we’d probably want to
build something into the language. Another way to go is to
look at models where there are parameters associated with data.
Those can often be factored.

The execution time for a gradient is split something like 70/30 between
constructing the expression graph and propagating derivatives. Three
cores might get that 70 down to 35, but that’s still not going to give
you a 2x speedup overall.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Parallelizing individual chains
parts:
Kevin knows what he’s doing, so I’m guessing he has
a 12+ core machine and wants to run 4 chains with
3 cores/chain.

And he’s not the only one who asked for this. We
mumble something about this line of optimization in our
recent scalability-based grant proposals, but don’t have
any concrete plans.

The closest I know to something doing serious parallelization
is Chad Sherer’s Passage sampler, but that’s only Gibbs for
BUGS-like directed graphical models.

There’s also the possibility for some models of using
parallel matrix libs and parallel ODE solvers. We’ve gotten
to the point of optimization where we’re calling them with
double values rather than autodiffing their algorithms. But
that only helps with models using those functions.

- Bob

messages.author: a8b6459b77c849fe
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Parallelizing individual chains
parts:
On Monday, February 2, 2015 at 12:55:53 PM UTC-7, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> The execution time for a gradient is split something like 70/30 between
> constructing the expression graph and propagating derivatives.

So getting rid of that effort in constructing the expression graph would be a big win all by itself. I haven't dug into the autodiff code, so I may be missing something, but can't we avoid this expensive expression tree construction altogether using source-code transformation instead of operator overloading?

Furthermore, if the model is expressed such that there is no overwriting of intermediate values through which the derivative computation propagates -- that is, you follow a single-assignment discipline for everything other than indexing variables in for loops -- the source-code translation approach is pretty straightforward. Every model I've ever written has satisfied this restriction. The only apparent exception would be summing the contributions to the log joint probability, but there's a straightforward source-code transformation for that, too.

C++ isn't the best language for this kind of symbolic manipulation, so I have in mind writing a program in something like Haskell that would take a .stan file and output C++ code to compute the log joint probability and its gradient. Does this sound reasonable?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Parallelizing individual chains
parts:
> On Feb 2, 2015, at 6:33 PM, Kevin Van Horn <ke...@ksvanhorn.com> wrote:
>
> On Monday, February 2, 2015 at 12:55:53 PM UTC-7, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> The execution time for a gradient is split something like 70/30 between
>> constructing the expression graph and propagating derivatives.
>
> So getting rid of that effort in constructing the expression graph would be a big win all by itself. I haven't dug into the autodiff code, so I may be missing something, but can't we avoid this expensive expression tree construction altogether using source-code transformation instead of operator overloading?

The answer is “yes, but”. There’s a big literature on
this — the Wikipedia’s a good start and autodiff.org
is OK.

Matt Hoffman’s very interested in doing this, which is
a very good sign it’s a good idea.

> Furthermore, if the model is expressed such that there is no overwriting of intermediate values through which the derivative computation propagates -- that is, you follow a single-assignment discipline for everything other than indexing variables in for loops -- the source-code translation approach is pretty straightforward.

Correct. I’m not sure reassignment is impossible for
code generation, but as you imagine, it’d be tricky.

You also have to be careful that there aren’t any
quantities dependent on parameters in conditionals (either
in the Stan code or in any function that’s autodiffed).

Matrices are tricky because you can’t rely on element-wise
autodiff. There will also be issues with nested solving as
used in the ODE solver (though this might be easier with
code gen — I haven’t really thought about it).

Some of the partials themselves involve little iterative
programs, but presumably you could code generate function calls.

We do a lot of optimization with metaprogramming and vectorization,
but presumably all that could be done with code generation too.

I have no idea how hard second- or higher-order autodiff would
be to code generate for.

And source code transformation, especially with syntactic
limitations, isn’t so convenient in a library, but it
doesn’t sound like that’s such a big deal for your use case.

> Every model I've ever written has satisfied this restriction. The only apparent exception would be summing the contributions to the log joint probability, but there's a straightforward source-code transformation for that, too.
>
> C++ isn't the best language for this kind of symbolic manipulation, so I have in mind writing a program in something like Haskell that would take a .stan file and output C++ code to compute the log joint probability and its gradient. Does this sound reasonable?

I know of two others who have gone that route (generating C++
from Haskell): Chad Scherer for his Passage sampler and Hal Daume III
for his Hierarchical Bayesian Compiler. Both used Gibbs.

You might also want to check out Theano, which does something
like analytical gradients (not quite code transformation).

Stan’s HMC and optimization code just rely on the models doing
the right thing for autodiff. It’d be relatively easy (compared to
rebuilding Stan’s autodiff based on code gen) to provide a different
way of code generating a model from what we do now.

- Bob
